openers.statherian-period: The Statherian marks the start of a long, quiet stretch sometimes called Earth's Middle Ages, a span from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago of tectonic stability, steady climate and slow evolution. Quiet did not mean idle. The oldest sand seas spread across several cratons, island arcs crashed into proto-North America, and in what is now Gabon, uranium deposits ran as natural nuclear reactors. In North China, the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes appear in the rocks.
openers.mesoproterozoic-era: The Mesoproterozoic is when the first algae turned sunlight into food. Around 1.6 billion years ago some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria and gained photosynthesis, and India's Chitrakoot Formation preserves the earliest known red algae. Oxygen may have risen briefly to about 4% of present levels. Columbia began to break apart, great igneous provinces flooded the continents, and in Africa a series of orogenies ran on until Rodinia was assembled about 1,000 million years ago.
openers.calymmian-period: The Calymmian is a period of new life and a fraying supercontinent. Eukaryotes took cyanobacteria inside their cells and became the first algae, and odd forms like Horodyskia, a string of beads on a thread, appeared. Oxygen may have pulsed briefly upward. Meanwhile Columbia began to fragment, rifts opened along the margins of Laurentia and other continents, and a deep rift basin on Laurentia's edge filled with the mud of the Belt Supergroup.
openers.ectasian-period: In the Ectasian, one supercontinent finished falling apart and the next began to form. A large igneous province about 1,380 million years ago marks Nuna's breakup, and from about 1,270 million years ago a massive igneous event spread across 2.7 million km² of the Canadian Shield. Fragments of the old supercontinent then began colliding to build Rodinia. Through it all, stromatolites reached their greatest abundance and diversity.

reviews.orosirian-period: The Orosirian is the period when Columbia came together. Collision after collision, from the Trans-Hudson and Penokean in North America to the Svecofennian in Scandinavia and the Glenburgh and Capricorn in Australia, stitched cratons into Laurentia, Baltica and a supercontinent that kept growing at its edges. Two giant impacts, Vredefort and Sudbury, struck its crust. In the oceans, banded iron formations largely vanished as the deep sea took up oxygen, while Gunflint microbes and the coiled Grypania show life adjusting to the new world.
reviews.statherian-period: The Statherian set the tone of the long, stable Boring Billion, yet it was full of firsts. Sand seas spread across the cratons, and the Yavapai and Mazatzal arcs added new crust to southern Laurentia. In Gabon, natural reactors ran on uranium for a time. Most important for later life, the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes appear in North China, a sign that life in a low-oxygen world was not purely microbial.
reviews.calymmian-period: The Calymmian ties the rise of algae to a planet in slow transition. Eukaryotes that captured cyanobacteria became the first algae, red algal mats grew in India, and Horodyskia and the Volyn microfossils show eukaryotes branching out, even into the deep biosphere. Brief pulses of oxygen may have helped them. On the continents Columbia began to fragment, the Belt Basin filled on Laurentia's edge, and great batholiths rose in what is now the southwestern United States.

prot-031.title: The early Ruker orogeny shapes Antarctica
prot-031.text: Part of Antarctica was once joined to a continent no one has identified. The early Ruker orogeny was mountain building that marked a key event in Antarctica's assembly. It joined East Antarctica to an unknown continental block as Columbia formed, between about 2.0 and 1.7 billion years ago. The other block is still unidentified, but the collision left its mark on the rocks beneath the ice.

prot-035.title: The Nagssugtoqidian orogeny in Greenland
prot-035.text: Greenland's ice hides the scar of a long-lost ocean. In the Nagssugtoqidian orogeny, mountain building formed the northern boundary of the mainly Archean North Atlantic craton. Island-arc terranes and two possible sutures, the seams where colliding plates joined, record subduction zones that have since vanished. It was one of the orogens that sutured Laurentia's cratonic blocks within Columbia.

prot-036.title: The Circum-Superior large igneous province
prot-036.text:
A ring of ancient magma more than 3,400 km long wraps around Canada's oldest craton. Between 1,884 and 1,870 million years ago, widespread mafic and ultramafic magma built the Circum-Superior Belt, a large igneous province, along the Superior craton's margin. Its dikes, sills and lavas stretch from Manitoba to Labrador and were emplaced in an extremely short geological time.

It erupted while the Trans-Hudson, New Quebec and Penokean orogenies surrounded the craton. In the Labrador Trough, its 1,880-million-year-old event covered about 30,000 km². Its origin is unclear, and proposals include rifting, mantle plumes and microcontinent breakup. It hosts major copper, nickel and platinum-group deposits, including Manitoba's Thompson nickel belt, and a rare Proterozoic komatiite belt.

prot-037.title: The Wopmay orogeny, plate tectonics in action
prot-037.text: Northern Canada preserves a textbook case of plates colliding. The Hottah terrane, a continental arc of volcanoes, collided with the Archean Slave Craton, closing the Coronation Ocean between them. The belt it left is about 500 km long and 200 km wide, and Great Bear arc magma kept erupting until about 1.84 billion years ago. Its oceanic crust, island arcs and colliding continents show that modern plate-tectonic forces were at work in the early Proterozoic.

prot-038.title: The Gunflint chert microfossils
prot-038.text:
On the north shore of Lake Superior, black chert holds a snapshot of microbial life. Layers of it, set in banded iron formation, preserve microfossils of microbes like cyanobacteria. The rock is built of stromatolites, and in Ontario some cyanobacterial colonies have turned to jasper, a red form of silica.

The fossils carry a message about the air. This microbiota shows that photosynthesis was under way and that the atmosphere held enough oxygen to sustain microbial life. Uranium–lead dating gives a consensus age of about 1.878 billion years, and interbedded ash layers date to 1.86–1.99 billion.

prot-039.title: Grypania, a coil of uncertain nature
prot-039.text: A coiled ribbon over a centimeter long is one of the most common large fossils of the Proterozoic. Grypania's oldest probable specimens date to about 1870 million years ago, redated from 2100 million, and the genus lasted into the Ediacaran. What it was is uncertain: a giant bacterium, a bacterial colony or a eukaryotic alga. If it was an alga, eukaryotes with organelles, specialized parts inside the cell, had already evolved.

prot-040.title: The Penokean orogeny around Lake Superior
prot-040.text: The Great Lakes region carries the crumpled record of a collision. Mountain building struck the Lake Superior area, in an embayment on the southern margin of the Superior Craton. A collision between two crustal domains drove rock northward in thrusts and folds, and reactivated the Great Lakes tectonic zone. It was one of the orogens of 1.9–1.8 billion years ago that sutured Laurentia's blocks during Columbia's assembly.

prot-041.title: Viruses that prey on bacteria
prot-041.text: Viruses are among life's oldest companions. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, emerged before, or soon after, the lineages of prokaryotes and eukaryotes diverged. Prokaryotes are cells without a nucleus; eukaryotes have one. The date given for this split is about 1.85 billion years ago. That makes bacterial viruses at least as old as the great division of cellular life.

prot-042.title: Banded iron formations disappear
prot-042.text:
After more than a billion years, the striped iron rocks suddenly stop. Banded iron formations largely vanish from the rock record worldwide after 1.85 billion years ago. Their end is read as the oxygenation of the deep ocean, once the iron dissolved in seawater had been oxidized and dropped out.

Before then, the ocean was persistently iron-rich, with possible intervals of euxinia, oxygen-free water laced with sulfide. The only extensive iron formations laid down later are tied to Cryogenian glacial deposits. An odd coincidence marks the turning point: a 10 km asteroid struck water about 1,000 m deep 1.849 billion years ago, at the same time as a pause in iron-formation deposition.

prot-043.title: The Trans-North China Orogen
prot-043.text: When did North China become one block? Its Eastern and Western Blocks collided over a subduction zone, forming the Trans-North China Orogen, and Zhao ties this to Columbia's assembly about 1.85 billion years ago. Kusky instead dates the joining to 2.5–2.3 billion years ago and reads the later event as a collision with Columbia. Earlier, about 1.95 billion years ago, the Yinshan and Ordos blocks collided to form the Western Block and the Khondalite Belt. The dispute is unresolved.

prot-044.title: The Sudbury impact
prot-044.text:
One of Canada's richest mining districts sits inside a 1.85-billion-year-old crater. A chondritic bolide, a stony asteroid 10–15 km wide, struck the Nuna supercontinent in what is now Ontario. It left one of the oldest and largest known impact structures, and its debris would have been scattered across the globe.

The Sudbury Igneous Complex formed at the same time, and its ores hold nickel, copper, platinum-group metals, gold and silver. The blow may have reached the seas as well. Some propose that it mixed the layered ocean through tsunamis, vaporized seawater and runoff from wrecked continental margins. It was one of the two largest known impacts of the Orosirian, near the period's end, alongside {{ref:prot-026}}.

prot-045.title: The Capricorn orogeny reworks Western Australia
prot-045.text: Even after two cratons joined, the crust between them kept churning. The Capricorn orogeny followed the collision of the Pilbara Craton and Glenburgh Terrane with the Yilgarn craton. It was the most important and widespread of the four orogenies that shaped the Gascoyne Complex, marked by reworking inside the continent. Voluminous Moorarie granites intruded the complex, and flood basalts erupted in the Yerrida Basin around 1830 million years ago.

prot-046.title: Columbia keeps growing at its edges
prot-046.text:
A supercontinent does not stop growing once it forms. After its final assembly about 1.82 billion years ago, Columbia kept growing until 1.5 billion years ago, as subduction fed magma and added crust at its margins.

A great magmatic belt formed along what are now the southern margins of North America, Greenland and Baltica. Similar belts grew around Amazonia, the North Australia and Gawler cratons, and North China. Extensive magmatism about 1,750 million years ago in Baltica, Sarmatia, Siberia, Laurentia and West Africa shows these cratons were linked, part of one slowly enlarging landmass.

prot-049.title: The oldest sand seas
prot-049.text: Deserts of shifting dunes are far older than any plant. Around 1.8 billion years ago, the oldest ergs, or sand seas, developed on several cratons. An erg is a vast field of wind-blown sand dunes, like those of the Sahara today. Their appearance shows that broad, dry continental interiors already existed, with winds strong enough to pile sand into dunes.

prot-050.title: The Boring Billion
prot-050.text:
For about a billion years, Earth seemed to hold its breath. From about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago, an informal span called the Boring Billion, or Earth's Middle Ages, was marked by tectonic stability, climatic stasis and slow biological evolution.

Oxygen stayed very low and no glaciations occurred, though a Scottish lake froze over in winter 1 billion years ago. The oceans may have been oxygen-poor, sulfidic and starved of nutrients, ruled by purple bacteria that used hydrogen sulfide instead of water, a so-called Canfield ocean. The carbon isotope record shows no major excursions. Mesoproterozoic temperatures may have averaged about 19 °C, some 4 °C warmer than today. The span ended with the breakup of Rodinia, a second oxygenation event and the Cryogenian Snowball Earth.

prot-051.title: The Yavapai orogeny
prot-051.text: The rocks at the bottom of the Grand Canyon were born as island chains crashed into a continent. The Yavapai island arc terrane collided with proto-North America in what is now New Mexico and Arizona. It was one of several arc terranes added to Laurentia's 1800-million-year-old core; related events include the Colorado and Central Plains orogenies. The Grand Canyon's Vishnu basement schists formed 1.75–1.73 billion years ago as island arcs collided with the mainland.

prot-052.title: The Oklo natural nuclear reactors
prot-052.text: Nuclear fission ran in Africa long before anyone built a reactor. About 1.7 billion years ago, natural nuclear fission reactors were generating power in what is now Oklo, Gabon. Concentrated uranium deposits started reacting after groundwater flooded them, since water slows neutrons enough to keep a chain reaction going. The reactions ran on and off, probably never above 100 kilowatts.

prot-054.title: The Mazatzal orogeny
prot-054.text: Southern North America grew by accretion, one island arc at a time. After the Yavapai collision, the Mazatzal island arc terrane collided with proto-North America in what is now New Mexico and Arizona. It was the next pulse in the growth of southern Laurentia. Between the two orogenies, short-lived basins opened as the crust stretched, and they filled with quartzite, once quartz sand, and rhyolite, a pale volcanic rock.

prot-055.title: The first multicellular eukaryotes
prot-055.text:
Life was learning to build bodies from many cells. North China's Chuanlinggou Formation, in the Yan Mountains, preserves the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes: Qingshania, Tawuia and Changchengia. Qingshania, dated elsewhere to 1.7 billion years, appears to consist of nearly identical cells.

Multicellular organisms with differentiated cells, performing specialized jobs, began to appear around 1.7 billion years ago. Multicellular eukaryotes probably evolved about 2–1.4 billion years ago, likely from colonies of single cells. Such finds show that Mesoproterozoic life was not purely microbial, as was once thought, even in the low-oxygen world of {{ref:prot-050}}.

prot-056.title: The Shoemaker impact structure
prot-056.text: Shatter cones and shocked quartz are the calling cards of an impact. Both turn up in Western Australia's Mid West, where a structure at least 30 km across marks an ancient strike. Its most cited age, about 1,630 million years, records a reheating of the granite. That reheating may date the impact, or only a regional tectonic event, so the impact's true age is uncertain.

prot-057.title: The earliest red algae
prot-057.text: Red seaweed has a family tree reaching back 1.6 billion years. India's Chitrakoot Formation, in the Vindhya Range, preserves the earliest known red algae, Rafatazmia and Ramathallus. Algae are eukaryotes that make their own food by photosynthesis. The oldest known red algal mats date to about 1.6 billion years ago. They show that complex, sun-powered eukaryotes were already part of {{ref:prot-050}}.

prot-059.title: The Isan orogeny and Mount Isa's ores
prot-059.text: One of the world's great metal mines owes its riches to mountain building. The Isan orogeny affected Queensland's Mount Isa Block about 1,600 million years ago, as large lead, silver, copper and zinc deposits were laid down. Mount Isa's lower lead–zinc–silver ore and upper copper ore lie in the 1,000 m thick Urquhart Shale, on one limb of a faulted fold. The belt is one of the 1.8–1.5-billion-year-old magmatic belts that grew along the North Australia Craton's margins.

prot-058.title: Eukaryotes capture cyanobacteria and become algae
prot-058.text:
Every green leaf on Earth contains the descendant of a captured microbe. Around 1.6 billion years ago, some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria as endosymbionts, partners living inside their cells. They gained oxygen-making photosynthesis through plastids, the organelles descended from those captured cells.

This was the second great act of swallowing, after the one in {{ref:prot-019}}. The new partnership produced the algae. Over time, they overtook cyanobacteria as the dominant primary producers, the organisms that make food at the base of the food web.

The fossil record follows. North China's Gaoyuzhuang Formation, about 1,589 million years old, preserves some of the first algae, such as Tuanshanzia and Grandilingulata. A diverse collection of fossil algae occurs in rocks dated between 1.5 and 1.4 billion years. Red algae appear too, as in {{ref:prot-057}}.

prot-061.title: A brief Mesoproterozoic rise in oxygen
prot-061.text:
In the middle of the long, oxygen-starved Boring Billion, oxygen may have briefly spiked. It is proposed to have risen at times to about 4% of present levels between 1.59 and 1.36 billion years ago. Gaoyuzhuang rocks in North China suggest a rise near 1.57 billion years ago. Formations in Australia, Russia and North China show oxygenation near 1.4 billion, though how global it was is unclear.

Early in the Ectasian, about 50–80% of the seafloor was oxidized, a share that later declined. Otherwise, oxygen may have stayed below 0.1–1% of modern levels, stalling complex life.

prot-064.title: The Volyn biota of Ukraine
prot-064.text: Life may have lived inside solid rock 1.5 billion years ago. In what is now Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine, exceptionally preserved microfossils formed in cavities of igneous rocks. They include filaments of varied shapes and fungus-like organisms. They may be among the first fossils of the deep biosphere, the life that dwells within rock and sediment far below the surface.

prot-063.title: Columbia breaks apart
prot-063.text:
The supercontinent built over hundreds of millions of years came apart just as slowly. Columbia began to fragment about 1.5–1.35 billion years ago, with rifting along the margins of Laurentia, India, Baltica, Siberia, southern Africa and North China. Widespread magma rose far from any mountain belt, forming suites of anorthosite, mangerite, charnockite and granite in North America, Baltica, Amazonia and North China.

Atlantica split from Nena, and North China broke away along the Zhaertai–Bayan Obo rift, where mafic sills record the event. Final breakup came about 1.3–1.2 billion years ago, marked by the 1.27-billion-year-old Mackenzie and 1.24-billion-year-old Sudbury dike swarms in North America. The fragments later reassembled into {{ref:prot-071}}.

prot-065.title: Horodyskia, a string of beads
prot-065.text: One of the oldest complex organisms looks like a necklace. Horodyskia is a string of beads joined by a fine thread, and its fossils span 1,480 to 550 million years ago. It is one of the oldest known eukaryotes and ranks among the first structurally complex ones. Its identity is unsettled: it may have been an early animal, or a colonial foraminiferan, a single-celled organism that builds a shell.

prot-066.title: The Belt Basin fills
prot-066.text: The peaks of Glacier National Park were once mud at the bottom of a basin. Much of the Belt Supergroup was laid down about 1450–1400 million years ago in a rift basin bounded by faults, on the edge of Laurentia within Columbia. Mostly fine mud, silt and sand piled up more than 15 km thick over some 200,000 km². The basin was probably closed or lake-like. Its rocks hold stromatolites and rich lead, zinc and silver ores.

prot-067.title: The Picuris orogeny and its granites
prot-067.text: A fifth of the Precambrian rock exposed in New Mexico and the Rockies comes from one age of granite. From 1.43 to 1.3 billion years ago, mountain building struck what is now the southwestern United States. Its batholiths, huge bodies of once-molten rock about 1,400 million years old, make up over 20% of exposed Precambrian rock there. Much of the mid-continent is underlain by the 1,450–1,350-million-year-old Granite-Rhyolite crustal province.

prot-068.title: The Kibaran orogeny in Africa
prot-068.text: Central Africa's mountain belts record a collision that lasted four hundred million years. A series of Kibaran orogenic events ran from about 1,400 million years ago until about 1,000 million, when Rodinia was assembled. From 1.4 to 1.2 billion years ago, it fused the Tanzanian and Congo cratons. In a narrower sense, the name covers an event about 1,375 million years ago that formed the Karagwe-Ankolean belt.

prot-069.title: A superplume splits Columbia
prot-069.text: The same flood of magma now lies scattered across five continents. A major large igneous province about 1,380 million years ago links Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia, Congo and West Africa, and it formed as Nuna, or Columbia, broke up. Magma of the same age in Congo and Siberia shows those two stayed close for at least 120 million years. Metamafic rocks of 1.37–1.35 billion years suggest a superplume, a giant upwelling of hot mantle, drove Columbia's breakup.

prot-070.title: The Mackenzie Large Igneous Province
prot-070.text:
About 3 million km³ of magma flooded the Canadian Shield in one event. Starting about 1,270 million years ago, it built a province of 2.7 million km², from Arctic Nunavut to the Great Lakes, linked to the Mackenzie hotspot.

It includes three famous parts: the Muskox layered intrusion, the Coppermine River flood basalts and the huge Mackenzie dike swarm, whose cracks fan out across the shield. Those dikes mark the final breakup of Columbia, the last stage of {{ref:prot-063}}.
